name: Lateral meniscus — body
description: Middle third of the lateral meniscus at the lateral joint line, between the anterior horn and the popliteal hiatus. On coronal PD/T2 fat-sat and T1 images it is a low-signal triangle with a thick peripheral base and a sharp free edge; on the most peripheral sagittal images the body forms the bow tie. The lateral meniscus is nearly circular, covers about 70% of the lateral tibial plateau and, unlike the medial meniscus, has no attachment to the LCL. Coronal images show its width and shape best.

normal_values.body_width_mid_coronal: about 11 mm on average; 15 mm or more = discoid (published cutoffs 13–17 mm)
normal_values.bow_tie_sagittal_images: 2 consecutive images on conventional (about 4–5 mm) sagittal slices; the count does not carry over to 3 mm or 3D slices

variants_pitfalls: Discoid lateral meniscus is the main variant here: 0.4–17% across series, about 3–5% in Western and 10–15% in Asian populations, and often bilateral (15–25% clinically; 97% of contralateral knees on MRI in one series of young Asian men; Kim 2020 review).

Call discoid when the body measures 15 mm or more on a mid-coronal slice or covers more than half the lateral plateau (SSR consensus 2026); the old rule of a bow tie on 3 or more contiguous 5-mm sagittal images should not be used with 3–4 mm slices. Report complete (whole plateau) or incomplete coverage, and any intrasubstance signal or tear, since discoid menisci tear easily.

The Wrisberg-type discoid (Watanabe type III) may be normal in shape: it lacks posterior meniscotibial and capsular attachments, so the posterior horn, held only by the ligament of Wrisberg, is hypermobile and can flip forward without a peripheral rim, mimicking a bucket-handle tear (Yue 2011).

Fewer bow ties than expected (one or none on 4–5 mm slices) means a displaced bucket-handle tear until proven otherwise: 97% sensitive in Helms 1998, 71% in Watt 2000. Look for the fragment in the notch or flipped onto the anterior horn.

Radial tears are most frequent in the middle third of the lateral meniscus (Magee 2002): look for a blunted or truncated free edge on coronal images and a cleft or missing triangle on one or two sagittal images. Adding fat-sat PD/T2 signal to these shape criteria raised MRI sensitivity from 68% to 89% in that series.
